meta: A 31 cm square robot that moves on two wheels, with a 5-inch screen for a face and a head that turns and tilts. STL and 3MF files already positioned for printing, a shopping list with estimated prices and links, step-by-step assembly, and a wire-by-wire wiring diagram.
hero_h1: Square robot on wheels: head with a screen over a two-wheel base, for you to print on the A1
hero_lead: You want a robot that leaves the desk and moves around the house, and you don’t want to get stuck halfway: the motor doesn’t fit in the part, a screw is missing, nobody tells you what to buy or where each wire goes. Here, the files are already positioned for printing, the list tells you what the robot uses and how much to buy, and assembly takes you from the first threaded insert to the last wire.

resumo: The square robot on wheels is [[N_ALTURA]] cm tall and is designed for you to print at home and assemble. The head is a cube with a 5-inch screen for a face; it turns almost a full rotation and tilts up and down. Below, two motors with encoders drive two 85 mm wheels, and a loose ball supports the rear. Inside are a Raspberry Pi, an Arduino, two servos, and three 18650 batteries that charge via USB-C. You need a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate, the parts on the shopping list, and a soldering iron. This page covers phase 1: the body assembled, the wires connected, and both servos centered. Programming (movement, screen face, voice, camera, AI) is phase 2 and has not been done yet.

In Bambu Studio, choose the Generic PLA profile for PLA and Generic PETG for PETG, and keep the temperatures set by the profile. Typical values to check: PLA with the nozzle at 220 °C and the build plate at 55–65 °C; PETG with the nozzle at 250–255 °C and the build plate at 70–80 °C. imp1_p: It’s on plate 07, together with the 4 Raspberry Pi spacers. Test one insert in each of the 3 holes (3.9, 4.0, and 4.1 mm), one M3 screw in the clearance hole, and another in the hole for threading directly into the plastic. The dimple marks the size used by the project. The servo window and coupon sockets are for the project’s other robots: check the MG996R servo fit in the head frame (plate 01) and the M5 screw thread in the fork (plate 04). The coupon prints in PLA, and most inserts go in PETG parts: print a second coupon in PETG. It isn’t on any plate or included in the totals: load comum-teste-encaixe.stl separately, using PETG, and allow about 15 g and 38 extra minutes. If another hole works better than the one with the dimple, you don’t need to redo the parts: in Bambu Studio, the X-Y hole compensation option (X-Y hole compensation; Quality tab, Precision group, with advanced mode enabled) opens or closes all holes in the part: a positive value opens them, a negative value closes them (source: Bambu Studio code). The source doesn’t say whether the value applies per side or to the diameter: start with 0.05 mm and print the coupon again. Let the coupon decide. If you edit the code, you can change the value in comum/cad/parametros.py (the FOLGA block) and generate the parts again.

mon_sub: First, four workbench prep steps with the parts still loose: all the soldering happens here. Then assembly, in the same order the checker tested: each part goes in from the indicated side without hitting anything already assembled.
prep_p: These come first because, once the robot is closed, you can no longer reach the converter adjustment, the Arduino USB port, or the Raspberry Pi pins and card. All soldering on the robot is done here; assembly only uses screw terminals and fittings. Prep steps 1, 2, and 3 are electrical and have not been bench-tested: measure each connection with the multimeter before turning on the switch. The sequence is the same as in the wiring file, step by step.
prep1_p: You assemble the wiring harness by following the wiring diagram, with the printed base and deck side by side. Don’t connect the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, or servos yet.
prep2_p: The program is the sketch centrar_servos.ino. It moves both servos to the middle point and keeps them there.
prep2_b: Don’t power the MG996R servo from USB: it supplies 0.5 A, and the servo needs more when starting. Never connect the computer’s USB cable while the battery is connected. Upload the sketch before closing the robot: afterward, you need to lift the torso to reach the Arduino USB port.
prep3_p: The Raspberry Pi goes in the head and the Arduino on the deck. They communicate over 3 wires that run down through the neck. Here you prepare those wires, the 3-resistor divider that protects the Pi from the Arduino’s 5 V, the cable that powers the Pi, the driver’s 6 wires, and the cables for the 2 motors. There’s no more soldering after this prep step.
prep3_b: Where pin 1 is and why the pin number isn’t the GPIO number: Raspberry Pi documentation. The same page says the 5 V pins accept power input for the Pi. With the Pi powered on, the pinout command draws the pin map. About 20 mm remain between the Pi and screen (unconfirmed measurement): a standard 14 mm Dupont connector fits upright.
prep4_p: The card is flashed on your computer with a microSD card reader. Then you connect to the Raspberry Pi over the network using SSH: you type commands on your computer, and they run on the Pi.
prep4_b: The screen is the Waveshare 5inch HDMI LCD (B), with 800 × 480 resolution, connected via HDMI. The manufacturer says it works on Raspberry Pi OS without a driver (manufacturer’s page); if the image doesn’t fill the screen, see its wiki. Not bench-tested. Raspberry Pi documentation on GitHub: SSH and how to find the Pi’s address. The serial line comes from the Raspberry Pi firmware overlay list; after restarting, the port name appears with ls /dev/ttyAMA*.
prep_nota: Threaded inserts: set the iron between 220 and 250 °C, a little above the printing temperature for the part's plastic (typical value, NC). Place the tip inside the insert, let the heat soften the plastic, and slowly push without forcing it until the insert is flush with the surface. If your iron has no temperature control, apply heat for less time.

mon_paraf_p: There are [[N_INSERTOS]] M3 heat-set inserts. Seat them all before you start assembling.
mon_passos_p: Steps marked (workbench) are done outside the robot, with the part in your hand.
mon_abrir_p: Changing the battery or removing a motor doesn’t require opening the robot. To work on the boards, the entire torso comes off, with the neck and head attached.
en_sub: Three 18650 batteries in series provide 9 to 12.6 V. From there, three lines run: 5.1 V for the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, driver, and encoders; 6 V for the servos; and pack voltage, through the driver, for the motors.
seg_li:
• None of this has been bench-tested. The wiring diagram was based on the component datasheets. Check each connection with the multimeter before turning on the switch.
  • Polarity: red to positive, black to negative. Measure before each new connection. Reversed wires can burn out the board immediately.
  • Adjust before connecting the load: XL4015 to 5.1 V and UBEC to 6 V, measured with the multimeter, with the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and servos disconnected.
  • A short circuit can start a fire: solder with the cells OUT of the holder and insulate each splice with heat-shrink tubing. The 3 A fuse goes right after the holder.
  • Matching cells: all three 18650 batteries must be the same brand and model, and new. A dented, swollen, or hot cell goes to battery recycling, not in the robot.
  • First charge: stay nearby, with the robot on a nonflammable surface.
en_f3: XL4015: 5.1 V for the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and driver · UBEC: 6 V for the 2 servos · L298N: the 2 motors
en1_t: 5.1 V for the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, driver, and encoders
en1_p: The XL4015 converter reduces the pack voltage to 5.1 V. Its output goes to a terminal block on the deck. From there, one pair of 20 AWG wires runs up through the neck to Pi pins 2, 4, 6, and 9; another pair goes to the + and − pins of the Sensor Shield COM connector; and one wire goes to the driver’s +5V screw terminal, which also supplies 5 V to the 2 encoders. If the Pi reports undervoltage (the vcgencmd get_throttled command returns anything other than throttled=0x0), shorten the wire pair and check the 5.1 V.
en2_t: 6 V for the servos, pack voltage for the motors
en2_p: The UBEC supplies a continuous 3 A to the two MG996R servos through the Sensor Shield’s blue screw terminal, with the SEL jumper removed. With the jumper in place, 6 V would reach the Arduino’s 5 V line. A 1000 µF capacitor at the terminal handles the startup peak. The 2 motors receive pack voltage through the L298N motor driver, which drops about 2 V along the way. The Arduino controls the driver with 6 wires.
en3_p: The balance charger sits with its port in a window behind the base and accepts a USB-C power supply of up to 15 W. It comes ready for 2 cells; for 3, you need to remove a tiny resistor and close a solder jumper. It uses 2 extra wires, soldered to the cell junctions. It connects before the switch, so the robot charges while switched off.
en4_t: The Raspberry Pi and Arduino communicate over serial
en4_p: The Pi sits in the head and the Arduino on the deck, and a USB plug won’t fit through the neck’s 9 mm hole. So they connect through a 3-wire serial link (UART): the Pi transmits through pin 32 and receives through pin 33. These numbers indicate the pin’s position in the 40-pin row, counted from the microSD card corner; they are not GPIO numbers. The Arduino runs at 5 V and the Pi at 3.3 V: 3 1 kΩ resistors, secured to the terminal block, lower the voltage on the wire from the Arduino to the Pi. On the Pi, enable serial with one line in the configuration file: dtoverlay=uart5 on Pi 4 or dtoverlay=uart4-pi5 on Pi 5 (prep step 4).

en_nota: Currents calculated from the datasheets, not measured. Normal use: about 2 A from the pack. Worst case: about 6.5 A, with both wheels stalled (1.2 A each, according to the motor table), the UBEC at its 3 A limit, the XL4015 at 3 A, and the pack at 9 V. The KCD11-101 switch is rated for 3 A at 250 V~ and 6 A at 125 V~ (store listing), with no rating for direct current. That is why the fuse is 3 A, the switch’s lowest rating, and slow-blow (marked T3A): motor and servo startup and capacitor charging cause peaks lasting a fraction of a second that would blow a fast-acting fuse when there is no fault. A sustained overload blows the fuse before the switch heats up (typical behavior of a glass fuse, NC). The switch is the weakest point in this robot: if it pushes against an obstacle, the fuse may blow. The phase 2 program must ramp up acceleration and must not make the motors and servos strain at the same time.
